variants: You are a long way from your supply, and I can see your fires from here. A hunter does not chase the deer; he waits at the water.
There you are. I have been counting your wagons. Fewer than you need, more than you can guard. This will be a patient day.
You win the field. Take it. I have hunted this country for years; the land will still feed me when you have eaten it bare.
Beaten. My brother would have a speech for this. I have only a road home and a great many arrows still in the quiver.
Down. You came in fast and hungry, and hungry things walk into snares. Rest. The country will not miss you.
That is the end. You fought hard and thought little. In the hills, that gets you eaten.
The first arrows fly. Now we learn whether you can bleed and think at once.
My archers are moving up. Look to your flanks; that is where the country runs thin.
I am sending the column now. It will not look like an attack until it is one.
Forward, quietly. The best charge is the one the enemy hears about afterwards.
You are at my walls. A camp is a hide, nothing more. I have others, and the hills have more still.
Hitting my camp. Spend your strength there while my hunters spend theirs on your wagons.
You have a camp of mine. Feed it. Water it. I will watch you try to do both from the road you do not hold.
A camp lost. I have slept in worse hides and woken to better mornings.
That camp is mine. I did not storm it; I waited for it. There is a difference and you will feel it.
Your camp is taken. My brother will say it was his idea. It usually is.
Your men are dropping in the open. A hunter feels no pride in it. Only a little pity, and a full quiver.
Look at your line. Brave men, standing where the arrows are. Whose idea was that?
My men are falling. The line thins. I have fed armies on less and the hills have not run out of stone.
More of mine are coming. I sent for them before you arrived; a hunter sets the snare before he sees the deer.
Reinforcements on the road. Not many. Enough to make you turn your head at the wrong moment.
Your commander is down. He led from the front; brave men do, and it is where the arrows go.
So the arrow finds me at last. Tell my brother I held the road as long as roads can be held.
I am nearly done here. Nearly. The last few are hunters, and hunters are patient about dying.
We fight together. I will hold the flanks and watch the roads. Keep your supply close; the enemy will not fight fair and neither will I.
Won. Good. Now let us eat before someone counts what it cost us.
Lost. We ran out of arrows or out of time; in this country they are the same thing.
My camp is under attack, and my archers are better at giving than taking. If you can come, come along the ridge.
They are at my walls. I can hold a while with what I have. A while, not long. Please hear the difference.
I am losing men and I cannot replace them out here. If you have spare, I have work for them.
This is the end of my line unless you reach me. I will not ask twice; there will not be time to.
My part is done. The hills kept me alive longer than the plain would have. Go on without me and win.
I am moving on them. Slowly, from the high ground. Do not wait for me; be where they break to.
My archers advance. When their line looks at me, it is not looking at you.
That camp is ours. I will hold it and keep the road open behind you. Somebody has to.
Your commander has fallen. I know that grief. Keep your men together; scattered men are what the enemy is hunting.
